newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro shares carried higher by Wall St surge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro shares carried higher by Wall St surge.

text.p: Europe's key stock markets opened firmer on Monday after weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs figures countered fears of an early rise in American interest rates and pushed Wall Street shares to another record.
"The whole interest rate story is looking positive right now," said a Frankfurt share trader.
While the U.S. May jobs report showed the unemployment rate dipped to 4.8 percent in May, it also indicated slower-than-expected employment growth in May.
The Dow responded by surging 130.49 points to close at 7,435.78, beating the old mark of 7,383.41 set on May 27.
In London shares opened higher, extending Friday's gains. The FTSE 100 was up 40.6 points, or 0.87 percent, at 4,685.6 by 0900 GMT.
On Friday, it rose 68.8-points -- its biggest one-day rise of the year so far.

Banks were again in focus, with Abbey National and National Westminster Bank, rising sharply after a report in the Sunday Times newspaper said there was pressure from NatWest's major shareholders for a bid or merger.
In Paris, French shares started 0.7 percent after a 1.06 percent jump on Friday, following fresh records on Wall Street. The CAC-40 index was up 22.70, or 0.83 percent, at 2,741.95 at 0900 GMT.
German shares set fresh records in early trade amid relief at Friday's U.S. jobs data which seemed to indicate a brighter outlook for the U.S. economy, and a reduced risk of an imminent rate hike.
"The whole interest rate story is looking positive right now," said a Frankfurt trader.

The 30-share DAX index was trading up 22.07 points at 3,717.36 points in the first half hour of floor trade, having slipped off an a new trading high of 3,734.05 points hit in the pre-bourse electronic session.

In currencies, the dollar was mired near a six-month low it set against the yen amid concern that Japan's trade surplus will be a focus of discussions at the the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrial nations later this month.
A barrage of comments from Japanese officials indicating they viewed the dollar's two-yen slump in Asia as excessive lifted the U.S. currency off its lows.
Broad-based yen strength, which has seen the Japanese currency also surge to a nine-month high against the mark, will, however, prevent the dollar clawing back too much ground, analysts said.

"The bottom line is that the yen is strong across the board and the overall bias is very much to buy yen on any dips" said Mark Geddes, the treasury economist at ABN Amro. "US comments which suggested that Japan's trade surplus will be a point of discussion for the G-7 triggered it."
The dollar was quoted at 112.52 yen at 0900 GMT, after falling as low as 111.80 yen in Asia, its weakest since November 25. 1996. The U.S. currency was at 1.7230 marks, from 1.7261 on Friday.

Concern about the potential for renewed trade friction between the U.S. and Japan was triggered after U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said on Friday the Clinton administration was worried about the potential for an upturn in Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. and a downturn in some of America's major export sectors.

The comments triggered speculation that Japan's trade surplus would become the focus for discussion by G7 nations when they meet in Denver between June 20-22. Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. leapt 163 percent in April from a year earlier to 831.48 billion yen.
Expectations that such concern might mount before the release of the Japanese trade report on June 17 and the G7 summit triggered sales of dollars, driving the U.S. currency down more than two yen.

Japanese officials were quick to step in to curb yen gains. Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said Japan would do its utmost to achieve currency stability, which would contribute to a sustainable economic recovery.
Tsutomu Makino, Japan's Vice Minister of International Trade and Industry, also weighed in saying Monday's rise in dollar/yen was excessive.

Also, Japanese Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa said he hoped for stable currency trading and said he was not aware that Japan's trade surplus would become a specific topic of discussion at the G7 meeting in Denver.
While these comments supported the dollar for the time being, traders said pressure on the U.S. currency was likely to emerge once more before next week.

The dollar was steadier in Europe, but off the 39-month high it set against the mark on Friday. Traders expect the dollar to remain supported against the mark, given persistent concern that European economic and monetary union will either be launched by a broad group of countries or delayed.
CURRENCIES AT 0900 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.7230 marks and 112.52 yen compared with 1.7261 marks and 115.23 yen in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 0900 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 40.6 at 4,685.6.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 22.70 points at 2,741.95.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was up 23.16 points at 3,718.45.
PRECIOUS METALS AT 0900 GMT

Gold stood at $344.45 in early European trade, unchanged from London close on Friday. Silver was lower at $4.82 versus $4.87. Palladium was higher at $235.00 versus $224.15, while platinum was lower at $485.00 versus $490.00.
